findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens returns incompatible types based on sync flag
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, this function calls fetch(...) and returns the fetch Response object. Otherwise it returns whatever refreshFunction() returns (which is provider-specific: a GaxiosResponse for googlecalendar, a HubspotToken for hubspot, an AxiosResponse for zoho-bigin/zohocrm, a fetch Response for office365calendar/office365video/webex/zoomvideo/larkcalendar). Callers then assume the returned value has the same shape as refreshFunction()'s return: e.g. googlecalendar does `res?.data` (GaxiosResponse.data) which is undefined on a fetch Response; hubspot reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (does not exist on a Response); zoho-bigin reads `tokenInfo.data.error` (axios response shape). Whenever the sync flag is enabled, these integrations will throw at runtime and break OAuth flows. The function must either always return a normalized shape (e.g. parsed JSON) or be split into two functions so callers know which shape they get.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse writes literal 'refresh_token' string into saved credentials
findings.body: When `refresh_token` is missing from the parsed response the function does `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`, mutating the parsed object. Callers then persist this object back into the Credential row (see googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97-101, office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:263-273 which spreads tokenResponse.data over o365AuthCredentials). The literal string "refresh_token" is saved as the OAuth refresh token. The next refresh attempt will send that string to Google/Microsoft/etc. and fail, and users have no way to recover without manually editing the DB. The function should either leave refresh_token alone (and let the caller decide what to do) or reject the response as invalid.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's dynamic keys are no-ops in Zod
findings.body: `z.object({ [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })` does not do what the comments claim. The bracketed expressions are evaluated once at schema creation time and resolve to the string `"ZodString"` (or similar), so this is effectively a single extra key "ZodString" on the object. It does not enforce "any property with a number is the expiry" nor does it allow arbitrary additional properties. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true the schema only requires `access_token` to be a string and otherwise accepts anything, so invalid/garbage token responses from the parent app will pass validation and be written into Cal.com's Credential table.

findings.title: Salesforce Connection is built from the expired access token, not the freshly refreshed one
findings.body: After the new refresh block saves `{...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token}` to the DB, the immediately-following `new jsforce.Connection({ ... accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` still passes the OLD access token from `credentialKey`. The connection is therefore used with the token that was just deemed expired enough to refresh. Salesforce API calls will be made with a stale token until the next request re-reads the credential from the DB, causing intermittent auth failures for bookings and contacts sync. Should be `accessToken: accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.

findings.title: Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method, including GET
findings.body: The handler performs no `req.method` check, meaning GET, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc. all flow through the same code path and are capable of creating or updating credentials. This makes CSRF-style attacks and accidental re-triggering via browser prefetch / link previews much easier. Add an explicit check that the request method is POST (or whatever the documented method is) and return 405 otherwise.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !==, vulnerable to timing attack
findings.body: The secret check uses `req.headers[name] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. String equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so an attacker with request-latency measurement capability (e.g. colocated on the same cloud region) can recover the secret byte-by-byte. Use a constant-time comparison such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(headerValue), Buffer.from(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET))` after length-checking.

findings.title: Find-then-create/update is racy and will produce duplicate credentials
findings.body: Between the `prisma.credential.findFirst` on line 62 and the subsequent `prisma.credential.create` on line 83 there is no transaction or unique constraint covering (userId, appId). Two near-simultaneous webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appSlug) will both observe no existing credential and both create one, producing duplicate credentials that later code paths (which use `findFirst`) silently ignore while the orphan still consumes app quota / shows in admin UIs. Use a single `prisma.credential.upsert` with a where clause on `(userId, appId)`, or wrap in `$transaction` with the proper unique constraint.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` is typed as `string | undefined` and the runtime value is either the second operand's string or the empty/falsy string `""` for the first operand. The codebase then uses `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED) { return 403 }` and `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && ...)`. This works for the obvious cases but silently treats the literal string `"false"` as truthy, and is fragile if either env var is ever set to a non-empty placeholder. Coerce with `!!` (or compare against empty string) and ideally name it like a boolean.

findings.title: Decrypt/JSON.parse failures are not caught
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt(...)` will throw if CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is missing (the `|| ""` fallback produces an unusable key), and `JSON.parse` will throw on any non-JSON plaintext. Because this happens after the secret check, an unauthenticated-bypass-shaped input becomes an unhandled 500 (and in some Next.js handler configs may leak stack info). Wrap the decrypt + parse in try/catch and return 400 with a non-leaky message; also early-return 503 when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset.

findings.title: redirectUri hardcodes 'zoho-bigin' instead of appConfig.slug
findings.body: The diff replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``. If appConfig.slug ever changes or the file is copied for another app, this diverges from the rest of the file (which still uses appConfig.slug elsewhere). Either keep using `appConfig.slug` or extract a constant.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse result spread can clobber persisted refresh_token
findings.body: `zoomTokenSchema.safeParse(oldCredential.key)` is the existing credential, then `key.access_token = newTokens.access_token; key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;` overwrite key with the new tokens, then `prisma.credential.update(... data: { key })`. However `key` here came from `oldCredential.key` (a parsed copy) — but the file uses the same pattern as office365calendar where tokenResponse.data (returned from parseRefreshTokenResponse) is spread. In office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264 the line `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }` will overwrite the real refresh_token with the `"refresh_token"` literal if the OAuth provider omits a new refresh_token in its response (common for many providers). Combined with finding #2, this silently breaks refresh flows.

findings.title: turbo.json lists CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY before CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, breaking alphabetical order
findings.body: Minor: in the new globalEnv block, `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is added on line 205, then `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` on 206, then `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on 207. The surrounding block was previously alphabetical (CALCOM_ENV, CALCOM_LICENSE_KEY, CALCOM_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, CI). The new entries are inserted out of order, which makes future diffs and merges noisier without affecting behavior.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh check uses response.statusText !== 'OK' which is unreliable
findings.body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` rejects any response whose status text differs from "OK". Many proxies / HTTP/2 responses return an empty statusText, and `response.ok` is the documented boolean for status 200-299. As written, a successful 200 refresh with an empty statusText will throw `HttpError(statusCode: 400, message: '')` and the credential will not be updated. Use `if (!response.ok)` instead.
